Description.Summary: Kimi OK Computer is an agentic AI mode embedded in Moonshot AI's Kimi chatbot platform, launched in alpha on September 26, 2025. It is a computer-use and browser agent capable of autonomously generating multi-page websites, editable slides, and reports from simple natural-language prompts. Built on the Kimi K2 mixture-of-experts model, it operates through a virtualized computer environment with over 20 built-in tools including a file system, web browser, terminal, and code and image generation. It is deployed as a web application feature (closed source) on kimi.com and offers freemium pricing with paid tiers.

evidence.quote: Kimi released 'OK Computer' on September 26, 2025, as its first Agent product mode.
Agent Mode of Moonshot AI's Kimi chat product, powered by the K2 model, categorized as Chat. Alpha release dated 26/09/2025.
Advertised for multi-step work such as building websites, web apps, and presentations, and visualizing large Excel datasets.

Practices.Summary: The Kimi Code team uses Vitest as its primary test runner, configured in a multi-project setup covering all workspace packages, the CLI application, and the VS Code extension. The CI pipeline splits the main test suite across a matrix of 5 shards with fail-fast disabled, ensuring reliability across parallel runs. Separate test jobs exist for the pi-tui library, the VS Code extension in legacy mode, and release scripts. Developers are expected to add tests to existing test files for the affected module rather than creating new test files.

Issues.Issue_Title: kimi -p: intermittent 'workspace is not materialized' from file-history endCheckpoint at exit
Issues.Description: In print mode, the file-history checkpointing system intermittently reports the workspace as not materialized at exit, revealing a race condition between workspace teardown and checkpoint finalization in v2.4.0/2.4.1.
On Windows, a computer-use input session lease is orphaned and the computer_use_busy flag persists across a full runtime restart, blocking further computer-use sessions until manually cleared.

Issues.Issue_Title: bug(compaction): pre-compaction token count disagrees with measured usage
Issues.Description: The token count used to trigger context compaction does not match actual measured usage, causing compaction to fire at incorrect times and potentially disrupting long-running agent sessions.

Issues.Issue_Title: [Bug] Kimi Web session pagination can exhaust the Node heap
Issues.Description: Loading large session histories in the web UI can exhaust the Node.js heap, revealing a memory management issue where paginated session data is not properly released.

Issues.Issue_Title: Duplicate stdio MCP server processes are spawned during one session startup
Issues.Description: Session initialization spawns duplicate stdio MCP server processes, wasting resources and potentially causing race conditions in tool availability during the session startup phase.

Issues.Issue_Title: `EnterPlanMode` always fails under an ACP client
Issues.Description: Under ACP (Agent Client Protocol), entering plan mode fatally fails because the agent attempts to read a plan file that has not yet been created, revealing a lifecycle ordering bug in ACP mode.

Issues.Issue_Title: [Bug] Session Markdown export corrupts YAML frontmatter
Issues.Description: Markdown export breaks YAML frontmatter when the workspace path contains special characters such as '#' or a colon followed by a space, indicating insufficient sanitization of path data in export logic.

Issues.Issue_Title: [Bug] Chat Completions streaming drops tool-call IDs from ID-only deltas
Issues.Description: In streaming mode, tool-call IDs are silently dropped when a delta contains only the ID field and no other content, potentially breaking downstream tools that rely on these IDs for request correlation.

Issues.Issue_Title: ACP mode aborts LLM requests at exactly ~10.5s
Issues.Description: In ACP mode, all LLM requests are cut off at approximately 10.5 seconds with an APITimeoutError, leaving non-trivial turns with no response and revealing a hardcoded timeout that is too short for complex agent operations.

Issues.Issue_Title: Agent presents a file-generation plan but does not create the artifact
Issues.Description: The agent describes a file-generation plan verbally but never executes the file creation step, exposing a gap between the planning and execution phases of the agent loop.

Issues.Issue_Title: Stale db.lock combined with Windows PID reuse permanently locks a query-store shard
Issues.Description: A stale lock file combined with Windows PID reuse permanently locks a query-store shard, causing the desktop session list to silently drop sessions until the lock is manually cleared.

Issues.Issue_Title: MCP OAuth doesn't request offline_access, so OIDC providers issue no refresh token
Issues.Description: The MCP OAuth flow omits the offline_access scope, preventing OIDC-compliant providers from issuing refresh tokens and forcing users to re-authorize on every session restart.

Issues.Issue_Title: OpenAI-compatible channel drops reasoning content when upstream uses OpenRouter format
Issues.Description: The OpenAI-compatible protocol drops reasoning content when the upstream provider (OpenRouter) uses its own response format, introduced as a regression between versions 0.41 and 0.42.

Issues.Issue_Title: When web server and CLI alternately drive a session, turn IDs collide and the message list freezes
Issues.Description: Using the web server and CLI in alternation on the same session causes turn ID collisions that freeze the message list in the UI, though the underlying data remains intact on disk.

Issues.Issue_Title: Default compaction trigger sits above the pre-trim budget, invalidating the prefix cache
Issues.Description: The default compaction threshold is set above the pre-trim token budget, so every compaction invalidates the prefix cache and increases latency for long-running agent sessions.

Practices.Summary: Issue patterns across the kimi-code tracker reveal four recurring engineering challenge categories: (1) ACP/protocol-layer bugs where the Agent Client Protocol introduces timeouts, lifecycle ordering failures, and streaming issues; (2) cross-platform and OS-specific bugs, especially on Windows, including file locking, PID reuse, and Remote Desktop performance; (3) context and memory management problems including token compaction miscalculation, heap exhaustion, and session ID collision; and (4) OAuth/MCP integration gaps such as missing offline_access scopes. The team uses GitHub Issues as the primary issue tracker with labels for bug classification and a maintainer /approve workflow for external bug fixes.

evidence.quote: External PRs are accepted only for approved bug fixes. A maintainer must approve the linked issue with an /approve comment. PRs without an approved issue may be closed without review.

Practices.Summary: The Kimi Code team follows a rapid-iteration development model with near-daily releases and a clear canary/stable release channel separation. New features that are not yet ready for public use are placed behind environment-driven experimental flags (KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_<NAME>) defaulting to off, allowing incremental rollout. The team uses a monorepo (pnpm workspace) and enforces engine-strict mode so that installations fail on mismatched Node.js or pnpm versions. Roadmap alignment is a hard requirement: only roadmap-aligned PRs are merged, and refactors without context are unlikely to land.

Practices.Summary: The Kimi Code team manages LLM integration through a dedicated llm module (packages/agent-core-v2) that handles request construction, protocol encoding/decoding, streaming, error classification, and retry policies. Prompt text stored in Markdown files under packages/agent-core-v2/src/**/*.md is treated as behavioral code and reviewed accordingly. New features are placed behind experimental flags by default. Failures are explicit rather than silent: unsupported features and empty responses fail rather than fall back silently. Media files are referenced as kimi-file:// URLs and resolved to uploaded IDs or inline base64 at request time.

evidence.quote: Treat prompt text under packages/agent-core-v2/src/**/*.md as behavior, and review edits to it accordingly.
Configuration is used exactly as given

Tools.Summary: The llm module supports four built-in LLM protocols: openai, openai-responses, anthropic, and google-genai. A Kimi-specific protocol and file upload mechanism are also included. The agent architecture uses XState state machines (actor-tree model) for managing agent lifecycle, turn flow, and tool invocation. Model configuration is handled through LlmModelSpec and LlmRequest serializable contracts with a ModelCatalog for metadata and default model management.

evidence.quote: Built-in protocols: openai, openai-responses, anthropic, and google-genai.
llm is a standalone library for a single LLM request. It handles the typed request contract, protocol encoding and decoding, streaming, thinking, media, error classification, and retry policies.

Stakeholders.Summary: The Moonshot AI model team trains the underlying Kimi K2 model using end-to-end reinforcement learning. The Kimi Code engineering team integrates the model into the agent via the llm module. The MIT AI Agent Index notes that Kimi K2 was trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning into a native agent that uses over 20 tools.

evidence.quote: The K2 model was trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning into a native agent that uses over 20 tools.

Others.Summary: The OK Computer agent (running on Kimi K2) uses an Agent Swarm architecture that can deploy up to 300 parallel sub-agents and execute more than 4,000 tool calls, coordinated by an internal controller that creates and assigns sub-agents at runtime. The agent uses an XState actor-tree model for managing agent lifecycle events. Events are classified as commands (imperative verbs), facts (past participles), or data streams, and must follow dot.case naming conventions.

evidence.quote: Agent Swarm uses an internal controller that creates and assigns sub-agents at runtime. It supports up to 300 parallel sub-agents, more than 4,000 tool calls.
Classify by receiver behavior. The guide says to classify an event by 'what the receiver does with it,' not by whether it carries a payload.
